2022_268_2022_summer_pd_boe_presentation.paragraph: Slides presented at the Troy School District Board of Education workshop on September 6, 2022 recap OneTroy summer professional learning for staff and summer learning programs for students. Staff work included the TSD Literacy Project with over 100 teachers spanning K-2, 3-5, 6-8 and 9-10, a Preschool Literacy Institute in its sixth year with over 30 staff members, and a four-day New Teacher Orientation. On the student side, K-6 Littera virtual tutoring reached over 400 students across the spring and summer sessions, and the Troy Summer Learning Lab enrolled 129 students from all four middle schools. A Data Dialogue on standardized test results was scheduled for October 4, 2022.
2022_268_2022_summer_pd_boe_presentation.page:
Summer Professional Learning and Summer School Update
Board of Education Workshop, September 6, 2022, Troy School District

**OneTroy Summer Learning (adult learning)**
Components listed: Technology Integration: Digital Media; Summer Curriculum Development; Administrative Kick-Off Meeting; Teaching and Learning Team Retreat; Cabinet Retreat; Board Learning with Tony Wagner; TSD Literacy Project; Pre-K Literacy; Troy Institutes K-12; High School Writing Institute; New Teacher Orientation; Math Recovery Institute.

**Principal Retreats and Admin Kick-Off**
Reflection on current state and next steps to sustain vision work; review of Mission, Vision, Values and Thematic Goals; level-specific meetings for bond engagement and communication materials; ALICE trainer training to empower administrators to lead safety training across all TSD facilities.

**Teaching and Learning Retreat**
Goal to design and review the work plan, with discussion of current state and next steps supporting the thematic goal embedded into content-area goals.

**Literacy and new-staff institutes**
TSD Literacy Project: over 100 teachers across K-2, 3-5, 6-8 and 9-10, with specific phonics work for K-2 and sustaining the Workshop Method PreK-10. Preschool Literacy Institute: over 30 staff members, the sixth year of summer learning for preschool staff. New Teacher Orientation: four days of professional development, a district tour, and time with mentor teachers.

**Summer program goals**
Provide access to all students in need using a flexible delivery model and grant funding when possible; community input identified tutoring as a key factor in family access to learning; district-level teams worked with building teams to design for local impact.

**Summer Program Summary**

| Program | # of Students | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| K-7 Multilingual | 130 | Morse/Troy Union |
| K-5 Multilingual Immersion | 75 | |
| 8-12 Multilingual | 15 | Services |
| K-5 Title I | In person 50, Virtual 15+ | Morse |
| K-6 Littera | 400 | Virtual/Contracted Service |
| K-8 Math Champs (Math Recovery 1:1) | 110 | Virtual/Contracted Service |
| 3-5 Math Classroom | 240 | Virtual |
| AYD Grade K-5 Math | 100+ | Virtual |
| Reading Recovery 1:1 | 16 | In Person |
| Math Recovery | 25 | Virtual |
| ESY | 200 | In Person |
| All Elementary Building Support | 30/building | In Person/Virtual |
| Troy Union Title I | 40+ | Troy Union |
| Morse Summer Nights | 150 | Morse |

**Featured program: Littera Tutoring and Math Recovery**
Virtual 30-minute sessions, three to four times a week, seven weeks total in summer, aimed at one-on-one tutoring to maintain reading and math growth. Over 400 K-6 students were served across the spring and summer sessions. Spring-to-fall comparison awaits the close of the assessment window; anecdotal reports from tutors and parents described progress, high engagement and consistent sessions.

**Community outreach**
Troy Union Summer Literacy Meet-Ups: four park events for K-5 families, with a traveling library. July 7 drew approximately 50 families, July 20 approximately 30 families, and the August 17 end-of-summer celebration drew over 250 people. A Padlet was created at https://padlet.com/kbush6/4tih3dz4g61ngl6m.

**Summer School Community Education**
In-seat enrollment (PE only): Session 1, 123 students; Session 2, 118 students. Virtual enrollment (Edgenuity): 1568 classes and 1002 students, with 75% of enrollment in grades 8-10. Math Honors Academy (in person, Bridge and Math 8 only): 27 students. COVID Credit Recovery, grades 9-12: 611 total courses taken and 399 total earned credits.

**Troy Summer Learning Lab**
Free program for students entering grades 6-8 using the Stanford design thinking process, opening with two weeks of immersion, guest speakers and field trips before defining, ideating and prototyping. 129 students from all four district middle schools participated, 21 TSD staff served as mentors and teachers, and the showcase of learning drew 170+ attendees.

**Next**
Data Dialogue on October 4, 2022 to review and discuss standardized test data (MSTEP, PSAT, SAT).
2022_268_2022_summer_pd_boe_presentation.verbose:
Presentation titled "Summer Professional Learning and Summer School Update," delivered September 6, 2022 at a Troy School District Board of Education Workshop. The deck covers two halves: OneTroy summer professional learning for staff, and summer learning programming for students, closing with a preview of an upcoming data review.

OneTroy Summer Learning components listed on the overview slide are Technology Integration: Digital Media; Summer Curriculum Development; Administrative Kick-Off Meeting; Teaching and Learning Team Retreat; Cabinet Retreat; Board Learning with Tony Wagner; TSD Literacy Project; Pre-K Literacy; Troy Institutes K-12; High School Writing Institute; New Teacher Orientation; and Math Recovery Institute.

Principal Retreats and the Admin Kick Off focused on reflecting on the current state and next steps to sustain vision work; reviewing Mission, Vision, Values and Thematic Goals; level-specific meetings for bond engagement and communication materials; and ALICE trainer training to ensure safety for all, empowering administrators to lead training across all TSD facilities. The Teaching and Learning Retreat had the goal of designing and reviewing the work plan, with discussion of the current state and next steps in supporting the thematic goal as embedded into content-area goals.

The TSD Literacy Project engaged over 100 teachers across four grade bands, K-2, 3-5, 6-8 and 9-10, with specific phonics work for K-2 and a focus on sustaining the Workshop Method PreK-10. The Preschool Literacy Institute had over 30 staff members present for the Summer Institute and marked the sixth year of summer learning for preschool staff. New Teacher Orientation consisted of four days of professional development, a tour of the district, and time with mentor teachers. A Summer Learning Brochure cover and an overview slide were also shown.

The student-facing portion, also dated September 6, 2022, opened with summer program goals: provide access to all students in need using a flexible delivery model and grant funding sources when possible; use community input, which identified tutoring as a key factor in helping families access learning; and have district-level teams work with building teams to design for impact at the local level.

The Summer Program Summary table lists program, number of students, and location: K-7 Multilingual, 130 students, at Morse/Troy Union; K-5 Multilingual Immersion, 75; 8-12 Multilingual, 15, Services; K-5 Title I, in person 50 and virtual 15+, at Morse; K-6 Littera, 400, virtual/contracted service; K-8 Math Champs (Math Recovery 1:1), 110, virtual/contracted service; 3-5 Math Classroom, 240, virtual; AYD Grade K-5 Math, 100+, virtual; Reading Recovery 1:1, 16, in person; Math Recovery, 25, virtual; ESY, 200, in person; All Elementary Building Support, 30 per building, in person/virtual; Troy Union Title I, 40+, at Troy Union; and Morse Summer Nights, 150, at Morse.

The featured program slide covers Littera Tutoring and Math Recovery. Delivery was virtual, in 30-minute sessions held three to four times a week for seven weeks total in the summer. The stated goal was to immerse students in one-on-one tutoring to help maintain reading and math growth over the summer. Across the spring and summer sessions, over 400 K-6th grade students were served. On data, the presentation states that spring-to-fall comparison will be possible once the assessment window closes; anecdotal input from both tutors and parents displayed student progress through the summer modules, high student engagement, and consistent sessions. The highlight cited was parent feedback about how much their child enjoyed the sessions and requests to continue into the fall.

Key celebrations listed: attendance was outstanding and students stayed engaged; parents and staff gave overwhelmingly positive feedback; and partnering helps support more students.

Community outreach is illustrated by the Troy Union Summer Literacy Meet-Ups, four events held across the summer at designated parks across Troy for all K-5 families, gathering families to engage around books and passion projects over lunch, and including a traveling library for book access. Attendance figures given are approximately 50 families on July 7th, approximately 30 families on July 20th, and over 250 people at the August 17th end-of-summer celebration. Feedback from kids and families across the summer and at the final celebration was described as overwhelmingly positive, with parents thanking staff for the opportunities and positive community engagement. A Padlet created for summer learning to keep families connected is linked at https://padlet.com/kbush6/4tih3dz4g61ngl6m.

Summer School Community Education reported in-seat enrollment (PE only) of 123 students in Session 1 and 118 students in Session 2. Virtual enrollment through Edgenuity covered 1568 classes and 1002 students, with 75% of enrollment in grades 8-10. The Math Honors Academy, offered in person for Bridge and Math 8 only, enrolled 27 students. COVID Credit Recovery for grades 9-12 recorded 611 total courses taken and 399 total earned credits.

The Troy Summer Learning Lab was a free summer program for students entering grades 6-8, focused on deep learning: students took part in an enrichment program using the Stanford design thinking process to undertake a project of their own choosing. Students began with two weeks of immersion filled with guest speakers and field trips to help them understand and empathize with various ideas and problems, then worked through defining problems, ideating and prototyping a solution. Participation was 129 students from all four district middle schools, with 21 TSD staff serving as mentors and teachers, and the showcase of learning drew 170+ attendees.

The closing slide announces the next step: a Data Dialogue on October 4, 2022, described as an opportunity to review and discuss standardized test data including MSTEP, PSAT and SAT.

2022_269_3_b_fielding_international_prop.paragraph: Education Design Services proposal from Fielding International, 460 Hilton Road, Ferndale, Michigan 48220, transmitted in a July 15, 2022 cover letter to Assistant Superintendent Christine DiPalato of Troy School District, 440 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, and dated June 20, 2022 in its page headers. The scope covers three phases of work to re-imagine middle school teaching, learning and physical space across Troy's four middle schools, running from August through December with a Discovery Report in October and a Learning Ecosystem Concept Design delivered in December. Total cost for Learning Design Services is $89,100, with reimbursable travel not to exceed $20,000.
2022_269_3_b_fielding_international_prop.page:
Fielding International, Education Design Services Proposal, Troy School District

**Parties and dates**
Cover letter dated July 15, 2022 from Fielding International, 460 Hilton Road, Ferndale, Michigan 48220 USA (fieldingintl.com), addressed to Ms. Christine DiPalato, Assistant Superintendent, Troy School District, 440 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. Signed by Michael Posthumus, Education Design Principal, mike.posthumus@fieldingintl.com. Proposal pages are headed "Troy School District Proposal June 20, 2022." Firm locations listed: Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Rhode Island, Singapore. A signature block for acceptance (signature, name/title, date) closes the document.

**Purpose**
Support Troy School District as it explores a new vision for middle school teaching and learning, shifting practice priorities toward strong interdisciplinary programming that also supports student wellness and social-emotional learning. Work begins by auditing staff and student perceptions, uses those insights to design a new learning ecosystem concept including physical space concepts, and transitions into process consulting alongside District leadership.

**Phase 1: Pre-Discovery and Framing**
Kick-off meeting, asynchronous data collection and information gathering, visioning and prioritization workshops, and virtual one-on-one 30-minute interviews with school leaders, ideally the building leaders at the four middle schools in Troy plus District leaders. Activities scheduled for August. Objective is a Teaching and Learning Audit Discovery Report.

**Phase 2: Program and Environment Discovery**
A multi-day immersive site visit with structured observations and informal interviews with students, teachers and staff to capture quantitative and qualitative data and identify mis-alignments between aspirations, physical learning environments and the actual student experience. Fielding also introduces exemplar school models; an optional and highly recommended visit by Troy staff to another innovative school is noted. Activities September-October; report development September-October; virtual report delivery October. Deliverable: Teaching, Learning, and Future Facilities Discovery Report, presented virtually to a "School Design Team" and other stakeholders.

**Phase 3: Re-Imagining School - A Deep Dive**
Two Building Common Understanding workshop days, three Design workshop days, and seven remote planning and reporting sessions, October-December. Sessions cover Who are the Students of the 21st Century, Youth Aspirations and Experiences, Science of Adolescent Learning, Teaching and Learning in the 21st Century, establishing a framework for a new school mission and culture, alignment between mission, culture, programs and physical space, cultivating student and staff agency, partnerships and networks, and re-imagining use of time, space and technology. Concept refinement November-December; report delivered December. Deliverable: Learning Ecosystem Concept Design.

**Future opportunities (not included)**
Preparing for Implementation and Change Leadership using "Process Consulting" as described by the Society for Process Consulting, proposed for January 2023 - June 2023 and beyond: Winter 2023, 3-4 workshop days; Spring 2023, 2-3 workshop days; Summer 2023, 1-2 workshop days, culminating in a Teaching, Learning, and Leading for the Future Guidebook. Architectural Design services are also offered; Fielding notes it is currently teamed with local architects in Michigan at Ann Arbor Public Schools and Portage Public Schools.

**Professional fees and expenses**

| Item | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Phase 1: Pre-Discovery (surveys, data collection, 1:1 interviews, start-up and visioning meeting) | not priced separately |
| Phase 2: Discovery | $34,500 |
| Phase 3: Re-Imagining Middle School - A Deep Dive | $54,600 |
| Total cost for Learning Design Services | $89,100 |
| Reimbursable travel expenses | Not-to-exceed $20,000 |

Travel covers airfare, lodging and meals for up to three to four Learning Designers on site visits, with some traveling from out of state.

**Terms**
Invoices monthly for a percentage of work completed by phase, payment due within 15 days; all travel reimbursed at cost without markup; printing or workshop materials reimbursed at cost without markup, noting some materials may already be on hand.
2022_269_3_b_fielding_international_prop.verbose:
Education Design Services proposal submitted to Troy School District by Fielding International, whose letterhead reads "Designing schools where learners Thrive," 460 Hilton Road, Ferndale, Michigan 48220 USA, fieldingintl.com. The transmittal letter is dated July 15, 2022 and is addressed to Ms. Christine DiPalato, Assistant Superintendent, Troy School District, 440 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, opening "Dear Christine and Leadership Team Members" and captioned "RE: Troy School District, Education Design Services Proposal." The proposal body pages carry the running header "Troy School District Proposal June 20, 2022." The firm lists offices in Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Rhode Island and Singapore. The signatory is Michael Posthumus, Education Design Principal, mike.posthumus@fieldingintl.com, and the document ends with a "Proposal Accepted by" block for signature, name and title, and date.

Purpose and framing. Fielding states it is pleased to provide the proposal to support Troy School District as it explores a new vision for what middle school teaching and learning might look like now and in the future. Based on previous conversations, the firm outlines a scope of work to facilitate an engagement and planning process to explore and then form a vision representing a shift in teaching and learning practice priorities better aligned with the District's objectives for strong interdisciplinary programming that also supports student wellness and social-emotional learning. The proposal includes phases that directly support implementing the community's vision of new middle school strategies. Work begins with auditing staff and student perceptions of the school experience, uses those insights to explore and design ways to transform the school experience with a new learning ecosystem concept aligned with the vision, including physical space concepts, and finally transitions into a process-consulting phase in which Fielding educators and designers work alongside District leadership and key staff for detailed planning, implementation and sustaining success. The letter frames the project as an opportunity to create a flexible and innovative school program and learning environments centered on what is meaningful and relevant to young people, and notes that upon signed acceptance work can begin immediately.

Phase 1: Pre-Discovery and Framing. Described as gathering contextual information to understand the current state of Troy School District middle school programs and their aspirations for a re-imagined future. It begins with meetings and data collection to learn about future goals while setting the dials for the work ahead. During this phase the Fielding Team hosts one-on-one 30-minute virtual meetings with a selection of school leaders to hear individual aspirations. Ideal interview candidates are the building leaders at the four middle schools in Troy, along with District leaders who will be engaged in the rest of the process. Format elements include a Pre-Discovery kick-off meeting, asynchronous data collection and information gathering, visioning and prioritization workshop(s), and virtual meetings and focused 1:1 interviews with District leaders. The objective is to collect data and observations to complete a Teaching and Learning Audit Discovery Report, serving as the foundation for common understanding of what currently occurs in school and what aspirations exist for change. Site visits and proposed activities are scheduled for August and include virtual kick-off and progress/status meetings, data collection through surveys and asynchronous resource gathering, and focus group and individual interviews.

Phase 2: Program and Environment Discovery. The main component is a multi-day immersive site visit by Fielding International team members, during which the team completes structured observations of the middle school experience and conducts informal interviews with students, teachers and staff members to capture quantitative and qualitative data on how teaching and learning experiences are delivered, and to identify mis-alignments between the aspirations of District and school leaders, the physical learning environments, and the actual student experience in school. The team debriefs immediate findings with the District at the end of the visit and uses time to plan following phases. Fielding also introduces school models demonstrating future-ready physical school designs and programmatic approaches to middle years learning; Troy's participating school leaders, and potentially staff and students, learn about schools and systems already providing aligned experiences. A school site visit from Troy to another school implementing innovative approaches is described as optional and highly recommended. The Phase Two deliverable is the Teaching, Learning, and Future Facilities Discovery Report, synthesizing information gathered, highlighting the core pillars of the future of Troy School District, misalignments between current practice and future aspirations, and prioritized areas of growth; it relies on first-hand data including interviews and observations from site visits and documents middle school learning models existing in other schools or programs. A virtual Discovery Report presentation to a selected "School Design Team" and other desired stakeholders takes place once the report is complete, ending phase two. Activities are scheduled for September-October, with report development September-October and virtual report delivery in October. The Phase 2 format list includes Discovery kick-off, visioning, multi-day on-site Discovery Visit, Discovery Report presentation, leadership kickoff, visioning workshop, student/staff/leadership focus groups and interviews, middle school program and facility observations, school model exemplar presentations and workshops, and Fielding team data synthesis.

Phase 3: Re-Imagining School - A Deep Dive. Fielding works alongside the District to facilitate a process helping students, staff and community members re-imagine the learning experience in Troy middle school programs, with two components: building a shared understanding of the problems and opportunities facing the District and its students, then conceptually re-designing the school experience. The Discovery Report serves as the foundational guiding document. The Common Understanding component includes workshops leading the School Design Team and potentially an expanded stakeholder group through learning experiences about Students in the 21st Century and post-COVID, reviewing research on the science of adolescent learning, the experiences and aspirations of today's youth, and contextualized place-based community needs, using models or case studies of innovative school programs. The Design component engages the School Design Team in constructive workshops to create a new vision for school, addressing how mission and culture may need to change, new teaching and learning strategies, student and teacher agency, partnerships and networks, and restructuring time, space and technology; both programs and physical learning environments are addressed. The Phase Three deliverable is the Learning Ecosystem Concept Design, a narrative describing ideal conditions for learning in a re-imagined Troy school, with images and precedent examples embedded. Format: two Building Common Understanding workshop days, three Design workshop days, and seven remote planning and reporting sessions, October-December. Session detail: Session 1, Who are the Students of the 21st Century (learn/reflect) and Youth Aspirations and Experiences (design/produce); Session 2, Science of Adolescent Learning and Teaching and Learning in the 21st Century; Session 3, Establishing the Framework for a New School Mission and Culture and Exploring Alignment between Mission, Culture, Programs, and Physical Space; Session 4, Cultivating Student and Staff Agency and Creating the Conditions for Engagement, plus Partnerships and Networks; Session 5, Re-imagining the Use of Time, Space and Technology and Final Reflections. Learning Ecosystem Concept refinement runs November-December with the report delivered in December.

Future opportunities, not included in the proposal. Preparing for Implementation and Change Leadership would use "Process Consulting," quoted from the Society for Process Consulting as an iterative form of humble inquiry and guidance in which the consultant works alongside the client to co-create solutions, advancing the client's growth and learning through authentic discovery and addressing social, relational, cultural and psychological dynamics of change. The proposal notes that as Troy School District prepares to invest millions in its new facilities, the opportunity to plan for new instructional methodologies is ideal. Key focus areas listed for Phase 4 are clarifying a future instructional vision, student assessment in the future, restructuring time/space/technology systems, finding coherence and cascading communications about change, building leadership capacity for change, re-imagining the successful middle school team, identifying and supporting early adopters, scaling adoption and improving practice, and sustaining success. The indicative timeline is January 2023 - June 2023 and/or beyond: Winter 2023 covering instructional vision, leadership coherence, cascading communications, student assessment and restructuring systems with 3-4 workshop days plus remote support; Spring 2023 covering leadership capacity for change, the middle school team, identifying early adopters and planning professional learning with 2-3 workshop days plus remote support, including establishing norms and indicators of success and beginning pathfinder prototypes; and Summer 2023 covering scaling adoption, improving practice and sustaining success with 1-2 workshop days plus remote support, formalizing short-term and long-term onboarding methods, a continuous improvement and success/failure-sharing strategy, review of cascading communication, and finalizing a Teaching, Learning, and Leading for the Future Guidebook.

Architectural Design is offered as an additional service. Fielding notes it is also an architecture design firm and can work alongside a local architect during Programming, Schematic Design and Design Development phases; the passage references "the opportunity in front of Holly Area Schools" and states that in Michigan Fielding is currently working in this capacity, teamed with a local architect, with Ann Arbor Public Schools and Portage Public Schools. The proposal also advises select web-based meetings in addition to face-to-face workshops to reduce cost and increase work consistency, with remote support often taking the form of bi-weekly team meetings adjusted to the District's needs.

Professional fees and expenses. Phase 1 Pre-Discovery, covering surveys, data collection, 1:1 interviews and a start-up and visioning meeting structured as a one-day visit/workshop, is listed without a separate price. Phase 2 Discovery, covering a three-to-four-day onsite Discovery Visit, interviews, focus groups and development of the Teaching, Learning, and Facilities Discovery Report, is $34,500. Phase 3, Re-Imagining Middle School - A Deep Dive, covering Common Understanding workshops and synthesis in one two-day onsite visit, Design workshops and synthesis in one three-day onsite visit, and remote planning and support plus Learning Ecosystem Concept development for facilities and program, is $54,600. Architectural and design services for new or re-imagined facilities and Preparing for Implementation and Change Leadership are listed as future opportunities not included. The total cost for Learning Design Services is $89,100. Reimbursable travel expenses are not-to-exceed $20,000, covering airfare, lodging and meals for up to three to four Learning Designers for on-site visits, with some Learning Designers traveling from out of state.

Terms. Invoices will be sent monthly for a percentage of the work completed by phase, with payment due within 15 days. All travel expenses are reimbursed at cost without markup. Any printing or materials needed for on-site workshops are reimbursed at cost without markup, with a note that such materials, including easel paper, markers and sticky notes, may already be on hand at the school.

2022_270_3_b_barton_malow_proposal_propo.verbose:
Proposal for Construction Services submitted by Barton Malow Builders to Troy School District for the 2022 Bond Program. The cover page is dated July 8, 2021, while every page footer reads "PROPOSAL FOR CONSTRUCTION MANAGEMENT SERVICES | JULY 8, 2022" and the Section 4 staffing plan carries the date 7/8/22. The table of contents lists Section 1 Project Approach Narrative, Section 2 Relevant Firm Experience, Section 3 Project Organizational Chart + Team Resumes, Section 4 Staffing Plan, and Section 5 Utilizing BIM + VDC.

Section 1, Project Approach Narrative. Barton Malow cites extensive knowledge of school construction and that its team spent over 30 successful years working in the Troy School District, implementing improvements at all district facilities including 12 elementary, 4 middle and 4 high schools, plus a new preschool building, the Early Childhood Center, completed in 2019. The firm would be involved in all phases from pre-construction and design to close out, working with the architect, engineers and district administration during design and offering feedback on constructibility, cost information and market conditions affecting labor and material availability and cost. Each project would be walked during design to determine existing conditions and minimize change orders and schedule delays. In the construction phase, meetings with the district's administrative team and building staff precede work to discuss schedule and phasing.

Design phase management includes establishing a design phase schedule with District approval listing activities needed to meet bid dates, regular design team meetings with published minutes, development of a set of Design Standards distributed to all Design Professionals, document double-checking to confirm standards are incorporated in bidding sets, and constructability review. The design process is broken into Schematic Design, Design Development and Construction Documents. At Schematic Design, information from the Bond Application is reviewed in detail and updated for scope changes, and the Schematic Design Estimate provides a higher level of detail than the original Bond Application. Through Design Development the estimate is updated and a very detailed estimate produced, with value engineering and bid alternates identified; Design Development is described as the most critical time of project design. A Cost Control Log is created at that point and updated during the Construction Document phase.

Cost control and value engineering rely on Barton Malow's in-house multi-disciplined estimating staff providing input on material substitutions, design modifications and quantity reductions, using in-house historical cost data and local market knowledge, with a "design to a cost" methodology monitoring items continuously rather than estimating only at the end of each phase. Minimizing interruptions in occupied facilities involves meeting with building administrators, developing a tentative work plan for administration approval, communicating the approved plan to staff, community and contractors, and zero tolerance for anyone failing to work within the plan's standards. Safety includes site-specific project safety plans, a Safety Manager conducting routine in-depth inspections in accordance with Barton Malow safety policies and MIOSHA standards and participating in all MIOSHA inspections, plus principles of leading by example with zero tolerance for unsafe acts, stopping the job for any safety concern, working with subcontractors sharing the same pursuit, and managing every incident to reduce performance impact.

Bid packaging is developed early with the project divided into area and functional phases, packages tailored to involve local businesses, long-lead-time items bid first and pre-purchase packages suggested where applicable, subcontractor data compiled by city, state and region, and a stringent prequalification process for prospective bidders. Barton Malow describes itself as the first to market to harness e-bidding technology, livestream bid openings and cloud-based plan rooms, meeting all State of Michigan bidding requirements, and notes it was able to solicit bids nearly every day of the State of Michigan "Stay Home/Stay Safe" executive order. The e-bidding process graphic lists bid advertisement, invitation to bid, pre-qualification, document distribution, notification and distribution, creation of the bid form, submission of bid security, submission of the bid, bid tabulation, addenda and audit trail. An "Unmatched Bidder Participation | Last 12 Months" panel reports 32 school districts, 157 unique projects, 68,856 solicitations to bids, 21,732 views, 4,089 bids received and 5.20 bids per category.

Workforce development is represented by the Barton Malow Boot Camp, created in 2016, a 6-week paid work experience program for area residents between the ages of 18-24 to learn skilled-trades industry fundamentals. The 120-hour program covers a historic overview of the construction industry and culture, financial literacy, OSHA and soft skills training, apprentice career path information, and on-the-job training in concrete and heavy civil work. Every boot camper is assigned a Barton Malow mentor, a skilled tradesperson on the project site, who spends 2 days per week giving career guidance and hands-on demonstrations. Participants are drawn from the Barton Malow workforce database, career fairs, local career and technical centers, vocational schools, technical colleges, building trade unions, employment service providers and labor management groups.

Procurement uses the software system Pype to create a submittal register as soon as construction documents are issued, identifying long lead and critical path items early; the submittal register is issued with the bid documents, long lead time information is requested post bid, and a long lead register is discussed and updated at each job progress and project team meeting. Change management is a disciplined four-stage approach; change issues are tracked as Pending (formally quoted, unapproved), Approved (formally added to the prime contract) and Approximate (known but not yet formally quoted), and move through four mechanisms: Potential Change Order (PCO), Change Order Request (COR), Prime Contract Change Order (PCCO) and Subcontractor Change Order (SCCO). PCOs are entered into Barton Malow's SAP cost management system, which tracks change documents, provides current and historical change information, and calculates the impact of changes in real time across each element, bid package and the total project. Barton Malow states it places no mark-up or additional costs for processing change orders, does not rely on outside agencies to validate change requests, and commits to having all final change orders approved, written and billed by subcontractors within 90 days of substantial completion. Non-responsive contractors may receive written notification, a corrective action plan jointly drafted, and contractual remedies including notice of contractual default and/or withholding payment, with meetings involving an officer of the Contractor.

Punchlist and closeout practices include constant site walk-throughs, weekly trade contractor meetings, pre-punchlists with required dates for corrective action generated ahead of the design team's official punchlist, commissioning documentation, close-out timelines per bid package typically requiring final close-out within 30 days from completion of all punchlist items, weekly close-out meetings for each contractor beginning at the 90% completion mark, and digital turnover of all closeout documents using systems such as AutoDesk Build. The Activation Phase covers start-up and testing of systems, training, final completion and occupancy, planned from the kick-off meeting. Final billings again commit that all change orders will be issued, approved and included in final billings no later than 90 days after substantial completion.

Section 5, Utilizing BIM + VDC. Barton Malow describes a holistic, value-driven approach to Virtual Design and Construction organized around discover, develop, analyze and share phases covering data collection and registration, content creation and workflow, collaborative analysis and continuous refinement, and information distribution and monitoring. Services include BIM Execution Plan authoring developed collaboratively with the design team at project start; 3D constructability reviews using the Design Intent Models to vet spatial configurations and clearances, accessibility, floor-to-floor heights, building system configurations and long lead-time items like steel, using a combination of Autodesk Navisworks and BIM Track with iterative reports to the design team; model-based quantity takeoff and scope visualization for material estimating and cost management; 3D coordination and clash detection for hard clashes such as a pipe hitting a duct as well as access clearances and equipment paths; 4D model-based scheduling linking model objects to activities in the live P6 construction schedule; site logistics planning using 3D models; reality capture using laser scanning, drones and 360-degree panoramic cameras to verify as-built conditions; virtual mock-ups and walkthroughs using virtual reality; and as-built BIM with data integration into the Owner's IWMS/CMMS facility management solutions, including submittals, operations and maintenance information and warranty data. On cost savings, Barton Malow states it has found contingencies can be lowered a full 2% when BIM is implemented, that this more than makes up for the upfront costs to create and update the model, and that BIM and the other VDC services listed are additional services that can be discussed prior to contract award.
